newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss WW2 probe wants more time for first reports.
newsitem.headline: Swiss WW2 probe wants more time for first reports.

text.p: A powerful panel of independent historians named by the Swiss government to probe the country's World War Two role said on Friday it needed more time for its first reports,which Berne had wanted by mid-year.

The panel of five Swiss and four foreign scholars, meeting for the first time, said they believed the government could grant them longer after recent dramatic Swiss steps to ease international criticism of the country's wartime financial dealings.

"The political pressure has relented for the moment," said Swiss economic historian Jean-Francois Bergier, chairman of the commission, at a news conference on its inaugural March 5-8 meeting in the Swiss capital Berne.
Bergier said the commission would ask the government for up to a year to complete two reports that he had earlier said could be delivered in the next two or three months.

The cabinet had asked Bergier for two fast reports on well-documented issues -- Swiss National Bank purchases of stolen gold from Nazi Germany's central bank and Switzerland's wartime policy of rejecting thousands of Jewish refugees while making Jewish groups pay upkeep for thousands more allowed in.

At the time of the cabinet request in January, the government wanted the commission reports as a basis for deciding how it would meet demands by world Jewish groups for a financial gesture of atonement.

But since then the government has gone ahead with a series of gestures, including setting up a Holocaust memorial fund with money from Swiss banks and industry, that have ended months of bitter attacks led by the World Jewish Congress.
"The situation has changed...With more time we can research these areas more thoroughly and set them in their historical context," Bergier said.

Bergier's commission is empowered by a federal decree to lift bank secrecy laws on historical records as well as look into otherwise confidential government files, powers Berne has never before granted to an expert enquiry.
Commission officials said the eight historians and one attorney planned to draft an initial strategy for their first year or two of work during their first meeting.
They were also interviewing some of over 500 candidates for a permanent research team of 20 or so scholars and hoped to finish the hiring in a few weeks.
The commission has a mandate of five years but expects to report at least every six months on its progress. Its initial budget from the Swiss government is five million Swiss francs ($3.4 million).
Its broad task is to chart the size and flow of waves of assets sent to the neutral banking nation for wartime safety as well as to probe Swiss business ties to Nazi Germany and its allies.

The commission's foreign members are former Polish foreign minister Wladyslaw Bartoszewski, Israeli historian Saul Friedlaender, Princeton University professor Harold James and Sybil Milton, a senior historian at the Holocaust Museum in Washington D.C.

The Bergier commission is separate from a panel chaired by former U.S. central bank chief Paul Volcker set up last May by Swiss banks and the WJC to sweep Swiss bank records for accounts left by victims of Nazi genocide. ($ = 1.477 Swiss Francs)
